answers.rationale: C best matches Jonah's repeatedly expressed preference for a workable afternoon outbound when there is no Monday obligation, while still reaching the destination at a reasonable evening hour before an 11:00 a.m. Tuesday review. It is cheaper and arrives slightly earlier than the otherwise similar A, avoids B's unnecessarily early departure, and avoids D's late arrival. Jonah does not force United when another carrier has the cleaner schedule.

C is the balanced late-morning option: it preserves a free window seat, avoids the very late D arrival, and leaves later than B for only a modest fare and arrival-time difference. A costs more and lacks Jonah's preferred free window. A 7:30 p.m. arrival is ample for a normal hotel check-in before an 11:00 a.m. briefing.

C is the strongest afternoon compromise: it leaves materially later than B, is cheaper than both A and B, has the longest and most forgiving connection, and still arrives at a manageable 9:15 p.m. for a 10:30 a.m. next-day session. D's midnight arrival is the late-arrival pattern Jonah repeatedly avoids before morning work.

C should lead because it provides a substantially earlier evening arrival than B or D, costs less than A, and still avoids an unreasonably early Monday departure. Jonah has moved travel earlier when a dinner or related pre-work obligation is truly important and reliably reachable, but the stated dinner is optional and A's 5:55 p.m. airport arrival leaves too little practical margin for a 6:45 p.m. dinner. The substantive work starts Tuesday, so C is the better schedule/value recommendation.
unsupported_assumptions: This treats a 5:55 p.m. airport arrival as too unreliable to plan around a 6:45 p.m. optional dinner; the dinner venue and ground-transfer time are not provided.
